summary: A request from MITRE for ARPA sites to help Georgetown University's library system. Sites could share an existing library retrieval system or the community could design a network library information system, possibly with a working group.

eli5.summary: A school asks if anyone can lend it a computer library catalog, or if everyone should build one together.

subtitle: A proposal to share library catalogs across the ARPA network using computer systems.

tldr.problem: Georgetown University was designing a learning resource center and needed a way to query its library holdings online. More broadly, library systems should be shareable across the network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes either sharing existing library retrieval systems or designing a unified network-wide library information system with protocols and a working group.
tldr.outcome: The proposal sought to enable library cooperation and inter-library loans across ARPA network sites.

today: RFC 286 documents early thinking about network-wide resource sharing in December 1971. It represents the ARPA community's recognition that computer networks could enable new forms of collaboration and resource sharing among institutions.

sections.title: Georgetown's Need
sections.content:
Georgetown University was designing a Learning Resource Center as part of its academic infrastructure. A key component was a system to enable computer queries of the university's library holdings, ideally accessible online.

Rather than building this in isolation, E. Forman from MITRE wrote to the ARPA network community asking if sites could help. Two options were proposed: either sharing an existing library retrieval system or collaborating on a new network-wide standard.
sections.eli5: A university wanted a computer system to search its library books and asked the network if anyone had one to share.

sections.title: Two Paths Forward
sections.content:
The first option was pragmatic: one or more organizations might already have a library retrieval system they could share with Georgetown. This would provide an immediate solution using existing technology.

The second option was more ambitious: design a unified network library information system that all sites could use. This would require establishing protocols, defining data structures, and potentially creating a working group to formalize the standards. The NIC was suggested as a possible focal point for design and operation.
sections.eli5: Either lend your library computer to the school, or everyone work together to design a system everyone can use.

sections.title: Network-Wide Benefits
sections.content:
The RFC recognized that most organizations on the network probably needed such a system. A shared standard would enable libraries to query each other's holdings and arrange inter-library loans across the network, multiplying value for all participants.

E. Forman called on sites to contact him if they had an existing system to share, if their organization was interested in participation, or if they wanted to help design such a system. The effort would build on the collaborative culture developing in the ARPA network.
sections.eli5: If everyone's library could talk to everyone else's library, they could borrow books from each other much more easily.

references.text: E. Forman at MITRE for information on library retrieval systems or working group participation.
